{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Sarcoidosis", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic urticaria with associated peripheral neuropathy (e.g., autoimmune urticarial neuropathy syndrome)", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Lepromatous leprosy", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides)", "confidence": 0.63}, {"diagnosis": "Systemic lupus erythematosus", "confidence": 0.59}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "The chronic (>12 months) pruritic rash involving upper body and face, coupled with symmetric palmar paresthesias, suggests a systemic inflammatory or granulomatous process with neurocutaneous involvement. Sarcoidosis is top-ranked due to its classic triad of cutaneous lesions (e.g., papules, plaques, lupus pernio), chronicity, and frequent association with small-fiber or peripheral neuropathy—including carpal tunnel-like symptoms—often without overt pulmonary involvement early on. Chronic urticaria with neuropathy is plausible given emerging evidence of autoimmune urticarial syndromes with neural autoantibodies (e.g., anti-TRPV1, anti-ganglioside), though palmar-predominant paresthesia is atypical. Lepromatous leprosy remains relevant despite low prevalence in non-endemic areas: it causes diffuse hypopigmented/erythematous rash with loss of sensation and early palmar involvement due to preferential Mycobacterium leprae tropism for cooler skin and peripheral nerves. Mycosis fungoides is included because early patch-stage disease can mimic eczema or psoriasis, persist for years, and rarely present with neuropathic symptoms via paraneoplastic mechanisms or direct nerve infiltration. SLE is lower-confidence due to lack of classic constitutional, musculoskeletal, or serologic clues (e.g., photosensitivity, malar rash, arthralgia, renal involvement), though subacute cutaneous lupus or neuropsychiatric variants could manifest atypically. Absence of fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, or lab data limits further refinement; urgent evaluation requires skin biopsy (with acid-fast stain if leprosy suspected), serum ACE/lysozyme, ANA/ENA, anti-neuronal antibodies, nerve conduction studies, and slit-skin smears if endemic exposure history exists."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Sjögren’s syndrome", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic idiopathic urticaria with secondary neuropathy", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Vitamin B12 deficiency neuropathy with coincident dermatitis", "confidence": 0.62}, {"diagnosis": "Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides)", "confidence": 0.58}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.604, "reasoning": "The chronic (>12 months) pruritic rash involving upper body and face, coupled with symmetric distal sensory symptoms (numbness/tingling in both palms), suggests a systemic immune-mediated or metabolic disorder. Sjögren’s syndrome is highly plausible: it commonly presents with chronic xerotic or papulosquamous facial/upper trunk rash (e.g., annular erythematous lesions, vasculitic purpura) and sensorimotor neuropathy—often affecting hands first—and may precede sicca symptoms. SLE remains strong given cutaneous involvement (e.g., subacute cutaneous LE, malar rash) and peripheral neuropathy (seen in ~10–15% of cases), though absence of anti-dsDNA data limits confirmation; however, up to 30% of SLE patients are anti-dsDNA-negative. Chronic idiopathic urticaria can rarely associate with autoimmune neuropathies (e.g., anti-MAG or nonspecific small-fiber neuropathy), though the duration and symmetry favor central/peripheral immune dysregulation over pure mast-cell activation. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes symmetric distal paresthesias and can induce hyperpigmentation or eczematous dermatitis, but rash is less typically prominent or pruritic for a full year without other hematologic/neurologic signs—making it plausible but lower priority. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) fits chronic pruritic patch/plaque rash on sun-protected upper trunk/face and can cause paraneoplastic neuropathy, but palm neuropathy is atypical (more common in advanced disease), and early-stage MF rarely presents with pure bilateral palmar paresthesia—hence included but lower confidence. Other considerations (e.g., sarcoidosis, Lyme, celiac) were excluded due to lack of supporting features (e.g., pulmonary symptoms, tick exposure, GI complaints)."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Sjögren’s syndrome", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP)", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)", "confidence": 0.71}, {"diagnosis": "Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) with anti-MAG neuropathy", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Dermatomyositis", "confidence": 0.63}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "The chronic (>12 months) itchy rash involving face and upper body—especially if violaceous, photosensitive, or periorbital—raises concern for autoimmune connective tissue disease. The new-onset bilateral palmar paresthesias suggest a distal symmetric sensorimotor or small-fiber neuropathy, possibly immune-mediated or paraprotein-related. Sjögren’s syndrome is top-ranked because it commonly presents with chronic xerotic/eczematous or annular rash (often on face/upper trunk) and sensory neuropathy (e.g., small-fiber or sensorimotor), frequently with positive anti-SSA/Ro antibodies not yet queried. CIDP is highly plausible given progressive symmetric paresthesias and potential subtle motor involvement (not yet assessed); though typically non-itchy, some patients report pruritus with associated immune dysregulation or overlapping autoimmunity. SLE remains likely: chronic malar/photodistributed rash plus peripheral neuropathy (up to 15% of cases) and possible subclinical serositis; absence of anti-dsDNA result lowers but does not exclude it. MGUS with anti-MAG neuropathy fits the insidious, distal paresthesias and may coexist with chronic dermatologic inflammation (e.g., IgM paraprotein-associated skin manifestations), though anti-MAG testing was not performed. Dermatomyositis is included due to characteristic heliotrope/periorbital rash, Gottron papules (may be pruritic), and less common but documented neuropathic symptoms—though weakness and elevated CK would strengthen this diagnosis. Key missing data limiting discrimination include ANA, anti-SSA/SSB, RF, cryoglobulins, nerve conduction studies, skin biopsy, and serum protein electrophoresis."}
